title: Recovery
lead: Failure models, STEAL/FORCE policies, write-ahead logging and ARIES phases.

sections.title: Failures and recovery responsibilities
sections.html:
Recovery preserves atomicity and durability when transactions abort or the system crashes. It includes actions during normal execution that create recovery information and actions after restart that use it.

The source distinguishes transaction failures, system failures and media failures. Its fail-stop crash model assumes persistent storage survives a system crash. Destroyed storage requires an independent backup or replica and suitable restoration procedures.

Updates occur in volatile buffers before data pages reach persistent storage. Recovery must distinguish committed work whose pages may be missing from disk from uncommitted work whose pages may already have reached disk.

PDF pp. 1–6

sections.title: STEAL and FORCE policies
sections.html:
STEAL permits flushing a page containing uncommitted updates; NO-STEAL forbids that. FORCE requires a transaction’s changed data pages to be persistent at commit; NO-FORCE does not.

NO-STEAL/FORCE avoids uncommitted disk updates and missing committed pages under its idealised completed-write assumptions. It imposes memory pressure and expensive commit-time page writes. A crash during multi-page installation still requires a mechanism for atomic completion.

The policy names describe permission and obligation, not individual events: STEAL does not mean every dirty page is flushed early, and NO-FORCE does not prohibit pages from being written before commit.

PDF pp. 7–15

sections.title: UNDO, REDO and logging
sections.html:
STEAL creates a need for UNDO because an aborted or unfinished transaction may have modified persistent data. NO-FORCE creates a need for REDO because a committed transaction’s updates may exist only in lost memory.

STEAL/NO-FORCE combines flexible buffer replacement with inexpensive commit-time data handling, but requires both recovery capabilities. A log stores enough information to reverse or reapply updates.

Log writes are typically sequential and can pack information for several updates into one page. The log and data pages are different persistent objects; a durable commit does not require every corresponding data page to have been flushed.

PDF pp. 16–18

sections.title: Write-ahead logging rules
sections.html:
Before an updated data page is written to persistent storage, the relevant update log records must already be persistent. This ordering preserves the information needed to undo an uncommitted page write or redo a committed update.

Before a commit is acknowledged, the transaction’s log records through its commit record must be durable. Appending a record to an in-memory log buffer is not the same as flushing it to persistent storage.

The source changes A from 1 to 8 and B from 5 to 9. After the update and commit records are flushed, a crash can be recovered even if the data pages still contain old values. WAL orders log and data persistence; it does not require immediate data-page writes.

PDF pp. 19–24

sections.title: ARIES analysis, redo and undo
sections.html:
ARIES supports recovery with WAL and STEAL/NO-FORCE. Analysis starts from a checkpoint and reconstructs transaction and dirty-page information needed to continue recovery.

Redo repeats the relevant history, including logged updates of transactions that may later be undone. It does not simply replay committed transactions. Page/log sequence information determines whether a logged action already appears on disk.

Undo reverses the remaining effects of loser transactions that did not complete successfully. The source introduces these three phases; a complete ARIES implementation additionally needs detailed log-record, checkpoint and compensation-record machinery.

PDF pp. 25–27

quiz.question: What does STEAL + NO-FORCE typically require?
quiz.explanation: STEAL can put uncommitted data on disk, while NO-FORCE can leave committed data only in RAM.

source.summary: Lecture 21 connects buffer policies to recovery, explains WAL, and introduces the three ARIES phases: analysis, redo, and undo.

limitations: The lecture introduces ARIES at a high level; it is not a complete implementation specification.
